summary: Petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 seeking various reliefs against Respondent No. 1 in terms of Power Purchase Agreement dated 25.7.2013 along with Affidavit. - _“(a) Hold and declare that the Petitioner is entitled to additional Capacity Charge of Rs. 43,47,09,038 for January, 2019 to March, 2019._ - _(e) Pass such other further order (s) as this Hon’ble Commission may deem and proper in the facts and circumstances of the present case.”_ 7. The matter was heard along with the related Petition No. 54/MP/2019 filed by the Petitioner, and the order in the instant Petition and the said Petition No. 54/MP/2019 was reserved on 6.12.2023. However, the order could not be issued prior to one Member of the Commission, who formed part of the Coram, demitted office. Therefore, the matter was relisted for hearing. Thereafter, the parties were heard on 13.8.2024, 18.10.2024, 23.1.2025, 25.2.2025, 19.5.2025, and the matter was heard on 8.7.2025, and an order was reserved. The order in Petition No. 54/MP/2019 was issued on 15.6.2026. reimbursement of such charges will be triggered for the Discoms. Thus, the responsibility of Procurers will kick in once the Petitioner has paid PGCIL, coupled with PTC having reimbursed the Petitioner towards payment of transmission charges. The gist of the submissions made by PTC in its replies against the Petitioner’s claim for additional Capacity Charges is as follows: - d) There is no delay in releasing payments to the Petitioner. Payments were made by PTC consistently on or before the due dates and, in many cases, even prior to them, at the specific request of the Petitioner. Further, the rebate deductions were voluntary, agreed to under Article 8.3.6 of the PPA, and were charged strictly in accordance with the agreement. Reconciliation statements signed by the Petitioner itself confirmed that payments were made on time. The allegations of delayed payment are misconceived. 12. The Petitioner, in its rejoinder to the reply filed by PTC, has made the following submissions: 13. The Petitioner in its Written Submissions dated 22.7.2025 reiterated the submissions made regarding the delay in payment of transmission charges in the Petition and submitted that there was a delay of 6 to 8 months in reimbursement of transmission charges on the part of PTC. The Petitioner has submitted that there cannot be an indefinite deferment of the obligation to reimburse transmission charges, and PTC cannot contend that the obligation is contingent upon fulfilment by UPPCL. Such an interpretation destroys the business efficacy of the PPAs and should be rejected. The Petitioner has submitted 20. Further, as per Clause 2(d) of the LTA Agreement dated 24.2.2010, the Petitioner 24. The Petitioner has contended that PTC did not perform its part of the contract as it did not reimburse the transmission charges/POC charges paid and claimed by the Petitioner, and placing reliance on the Hon’ble Madras High Court judgment in the case of G. Anbalagan v. T.N. Civil Supplies Corporation (AIR 2002 Mad 230), has reiterated that contractual obligation once agreed cannot be unilaterally varied. It is observed that PTC has reimbursed the transmission charges for the energy supplied by the Petitioner and has fulfilled its part of the contract. On the contrary, the Petitioner has failed to perform its part of the contract, as it has not paid the transmission charges, leading to the regulation of power and a short supply of power to PTC/ UP Discoms. 25. Referring to judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court _in Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India_ , [(2001) 2 SCC 41], _Jet Airways (India) Ltd. v. Sahara Airlines Ltd._ , [2011 SCC On Line Bom 576], and _Nandlal Singh v. Ram Kirit Singh [AIR 1950 Pat 212],_ UPPCL has contended that there can be no reimbursement of the expenses/ charges which had never been incurred/ paid by the Petitioner. As stated earlier, only after the Petitioner remits the transmission charges to PGCIL, PTC’s obligation to reimburse the transmission charges to the Petitioner arises. In the instant case, the Petitioner has not paid the transmission charges to PGCIL, leading to the regulation of power by PGCIL. When the Petitioner has not paid the transmission charges to PGCIL, there was no occasion for PTC to reimburse the same to the Petitioner. Therefore, we tend to agree with UPPCL’s 35. In response, UPPCL has submitted that in compliance with the Commission’s directions in Petition No.77/MP/2018, the Petitioner raised a Supplementary Bill reconciling penalties for the period from December 2016 to March 2019. This was duly approved by UPPCL, including the liability towards LPS, and hence no anomaly exists in the levy of penalties. UPPCL has submitted that there is no default on the part of the Discoms under the Procurer-PPA with respect to the Petitioner’s claims. Consequently, the relief sought regarding the payment of LPS has no merit. UPPCL has further submitted that the Petitioner’s claim for losses arising from curtailment of power by PGCIL is not attributable to any act or omission on its part under the Procurers’ PPA. There is no default on the part of the Discoms under the Procurers’ PPA in relation to the claims raised by the Petitioner. Accordingly, the relief sought by the Petitioner towards LPS should not be allowed. 38. We have already held that the Petitioner is not eligible for additional Capacity Charges and a refund of the penalty claimed for the period from January, 2019 to March, 2019. We have also held that the penalty paid “during earlier months” has already been taken care of in the reconciliation carried out by the parties as per the Commission’s directions in the order dated 14.5.2019 in Petition No.77/MP/2018. Therefore, the Petitioner’s prayer for LPS has become infructuous.
